@SamFerracin 
My biggest question was - should these assertions be enforced together with the samplex arguments ones? On the one hand, it complicates things a bit, and removes some future flexibility (say you want to extend to twiriling strategy - one set of assertions doesn't care, while the other does). A few comments and suggestions:
- I get your point that "this complicates things a bit, and removes some future flexibility," and I agree that this may be coming from the fact that more than one thing (samplex arguments and template) is being tested with the same test function. I believe that it would be simpler if these were different tests. In particular, I would:
  - Make two different test functions, `test_samplex_arguments` and `test_template_circuits`--one concern per test function
  -  Rename `assertSamplexItemIsCorrect` as `assertSamplexArgumentsAreCorrect` 
  -  Add `assertTemplateIsCorrect`
- "Looking ahead, I believe when we add the tests to assert the shape of the samplex item, ..." Yes, I agree on this too. And I'd be in favour of adding a third test function for that, since this is a different concern

Separate from the above:
If the test functions are different, there's an opportunity to simplify even further. Each one of them can have their own `SCENARIO`, you don't need to use `SAMPLEX_CIRCUIT_SCENARIOS`. And I suspect you could choose circuits that allow you to simplify your assertions even further. circuit.cx(0, 1)
circuit.cx(1, 2)
circuit.measure_all()

Readers of this PR may become confused because the terms `sampler` and `local` are overloaded:
- There are two samplers: the aer sampler and the wrapper sampler. Both are sometimes called only "sampler", and the reader is assumed to determine from the context which sampler it is. The executor is a layer between these two samplers.
- Local mode and local metadata - local mode is the wrapper sampler when it runs with a simulator; local metadata is the metadata of a pub result, in contrast to a program's result.

(Edited the comment to hopefully make it clearer) -
I think (and emphasis Tsafrir comment) that the calculation of the mitigated expectation value can't be in the same way that we calculate the projector expectation value without mitigation, with just multiplying by some factor (as we do in the Pauli case).

The current code calculates the expectation value of an observable that contains projectors by removing from the calculation any shot that will contribute zero to the expectation value (due to the 0 eigenvalue of the projector part). In a noisy case this approach is not accurate anymore as the TREX mitigation calculates the expectation value based on statistics of an ensemble of shots. The mitigation do not fix each individual binary string, therefore "throwing shots from the calculation" based on each binary string separately makes the calculation inaccurate.

In order to calculate the mitigated expectation value accurately, I think we must expand the operator in the Pauli basis, and calculate the expanded observable. Each Pauli term in the expanded observable can be mitigated, and because of linearity, the whole expectation value will be mitigated.
Important note is that such expansion might be exponential in the number of projector elements in the observable. This will result in an exponential classical computation.
In the future, we might think of approximations that can keep the classical calculation polynomial and still have a good approximation to the mitigated result. In the meanwhile, we can warn the user if his observable has too many (we can think what should be the threshold for "too many") projector elements while using TREX mitigation.

Note - also in the original TREX paper, in order to do a mitigation to a non Pauli operator, it is written that one should expand the operator to a Pauli basis and mitigate in the Pauli basis.

As I see it, we have two options to fix the issue.

## Option 1
The change in this PR, namely changing `twirling_group` from `"balanced_pauli"` to `"local_pauli"`.

Advantages:
- It fixes the issue

Disadvantages:
- Talking to Josh, it came up that "local_pauli"  twirls Clifford gates in the same way as "pauli" does, so it does it's job. However, it's less efficient than "pauli" or "balanced_pauli", because it needs to look at the content of the layer beforehand 
- It hardcodes the default to a twirling group that's probably not what we want to have--I imagine that when we expose this via the options, we'd want to have "pauli" as default, but then that'd create a breaking change (circuits with RZZs that were passing before do not pass anymore)

## Option 2
Expose `twirling_group` in the twirling options, set it to `"pauli"` by default, and letting users change it as they want.

Advantages:
- Fixes the issue, actually in a better way

Disadvantages:
- We need to make an exception to the rule that EstimatorV2 needs to support legacy features, and we'll support new features later.

---
Of the two, I prefer option 2. Any thoughts?

I was really having troubles wrapping my head around this PR, and I concluded that I was trying to do too much all at once. Therefore, I decided to take a step back (at the cost of making a high number of pushes, apologies for all the spam emails 😅). But now I'm at a point where I can clearly say what this PR tries to do.

### What this PR does

[see release note]
- `QuantumProgram`, `QuantumProgramResult`, and `QuantumProgramItemResult` now inherit from the corresponding classes in Samplomatic.
- `CircuitItem`, `SamplexItem`, `DataTree`, `ChunkPart`, `ChunkSpan`, `ChunkTiming`, and `draw_chunk_timings` are now imported from Samplomatic. Importing them from qiskit-ibm-runtime is still supported.

Example to understand the second bullet: Where I had `class SamplexItem`, now I have `from samplomatic.quantum_program import SamplexItem` ([link](https://github.com/Qiskit/qiskit-ibm-runtime/pull/3206/changes#diff-cc5f3a8f9adc768ea42145e2ebb7111e9bd7eb17874d331b6cde4a76e9ea869fR24-R28)). 
This guarantees that:
- Scripts that contained `from qiskit_ibm_runtime.quantum_program import SamplexItem` keep working.
- No deprecation warnings
- Discoverability doesn't break

All in all, nothing changes. To prove it, I have reverted every other change, including:
- Import statements in other files: all reverted back to what they are in main
- Tests: No changes in the test files

### What this PR does not do

There are a few follow-up steps that we need to take. We can either take them in this PR or in subsequent PRs. I'll let the reviewers express their preference, and I'll open issues if we go with the latter.

#### 1. Update imports
- [ ] Update every single file (source, and tests), replacing imports like `from qiskit_ibm_runtime.quantum_program import SamplexItem` with imports like `from samplomatic.quantum_program import SamplexItem`.

#### 2. Deprecate importing from qiskit-ibm-runtime
- [ ] `from qiskit_ibm_runtime.quantum_program import SamplexItem` should be deprecated. Users should just import Samplomatic objects from Samplomatic via `from samplomatic.quantum_program import SamplexItem`. 

There are a few different ways of doing this. One is through a deprecation warning like I had in previous commits ([link](https://github.com/Qiskit/qiskit-ibm-runtime/pull/3206/changes/6e94c9b3505c3999cc1342aaf2ea6091d17d5396..db2e2d9c8eef8c04cdbf1a440b67dab483f120c4#diff-08660ec084d53960e4ecce73969a20eb706c83132669b58bab5113bb1edbef49R42-R55)), which is fine but breaks the LSP. Another one is through docstrings, as Diego suggests, which does not break LSP but may go unnoticed by users.

#### 3. Remove unnecessary tests
If `SamplexItem` lives in Samplomatic, then it should be tested in Samplomatic. We can remove the tests. 
- [ ] Remove unit tests that target `CircuitItem`, `SamplexItem`, `DataTree`, `ChunkPart`, `ChunkSpan`, `ChunkTiming`, and `draw_chunk_timings`.

> Note that annotations cannot be mutated in python space.

The "safe" way to do it in Python space is to do it the way Samplomatic does it:
- Generate an empty dag
- Loop through the circuit, and append instructions to the dag with `annotations=[]`
- Convert the dag to a circuit

So that gives you a new circuit, without mutating the input one.

> `unbroadcast_index` and `get_pauli_basis` moved out of the estimator utils, but are now imported there. If they are used in both places, shouldn't we create a common place for them to reside in?

Thanks for catching this (somehow I overlooked the intermediate `compute_samplex_arguments`, which should be obvious looking at the new import in `qiskit_ibm_runtime/executor_estimator/utils.py`)!

Looking at options for such a common place, I don't see a good one:
* `executor/something.py` - originally deemed as the place for "utils share by the two families of prepares". Could be an option, but ends up more wrapper-specifics item into `executor/` (which conceptually is not so sound, and in practice reinforces import cycles on `executor` items)
* utils/something.py` - probably doable now that utils is relatively import-cycle-lean. Goes a bit against the direction of trying to use `utils/` as a last resort (as doing so increases the risk of it being a container for disparate functionality)
* a new module at top-level - it does not seem that helper functions merit such a high/visible location just based on import cycle optimization
* a new module inside an existing package - I cannot see any good candidate

So I'm leaning towards keeping the PR as is: it does increase `decoders/` modularization (ie. decoders no longer depends on wrappers, which was a source of cycles). It does increase the wrappers export surface a bit (it already has a large surface), but that direction does not seem to be a source of cycles at the moment and improving the modularization of the wrappers can be tackled separately.

> Overall I think this makes sense thanks @diego-plan9! I was also wondering if you have an idea of what can be simplified once we remove the legacy local mode code?

Thanks for the review!

It might depend which removal you are referring to:
* the one that allows wrapper to use local mode but not through sim-executor: it seems it might be just a matter of deleting the branching and `_run_legacy_simulation` functions.
* the one that allows non-wrapper primitives to be run in local mode: it would make `LocalRuntimeJob` have to deal only with executor jobs, and `QiskitRuntimeLocalService` to only understand executor jobs. This likely will lead to quite some simplification of their logic, but the pattern of "a primitive delegates on a service, and the service create the job" will likely stay (and arguably simplified by this PR).

Regardless, some simplification of the primitives `run` methods and general complexity can likely be achieved via #2874 (ie. if we model a "mode" differently, all the nuances the primitives have and fine-grain peeking into how that "mode" is implemented will result in cleaner primitives). > As an aside: is there a general rule to follow for when we want to use the full path in sphinx versus e.g. `~.EstimatorOptions`? I know this PR is meant to address reference warnings but just wondering what should be the best practice for these in general

On conventions in general - the sphinx syntax is at https://www.sphinx-doc.org/en/master/usage/domains/python.html#target-specification (target specification and target resolution). We don't have an explicit convention in the project - in general, we tend to specify via:
```
 :class:`~.MyClass` 
```
as this will:
* look first in the current module (via the `.`), which is a common case and saves us some characters
* just display the class name as the rendered link text (via the `~`), which is more reading-friendly

Regarding using the full path: in this PR, I used the full path in the cases where we have classes with the same name (ie. `EstimatorOptions`, `SamplerV2`) and sphinx is unable to decide between them. The PR is "reactive" - the first two commits add classes to the documentation and sphinx index, this triggers the warnings, the rest of the commits fix them, and the final commits removes them from the documentation (as we don't want them to be rendered yet, but will once we declare wrappers public). 

So an approach might be: keep using the without-path form until sphinx complains, and if so, use the full-path form for resolving ambiguity.

We experience similar issues when replacing xslow in the examples above with `qc.append(MidCircuitMeasure(), [0], [0])`.

In the first case (qasm3 exporter) we obtain an error, but it's not about the instruction definition this time:
```
qiskit.qasm3.exceptions.QASM3ExporterError: "non-unitary subroutine calls are not yet supported, but received 'Instruction(name='measure_2', num_qubits=1, num_clbits=1, params=[])'"
```

The second case (class preservation) is more similar:
```
Instruction None
```

About class preservation, note that the instruction name is preserved. This is important, because this is what makes everything work, although the server loads qpy payload that the client dumped. The server sees a generic `Gate` whose name is `xslow`, and this is enough for the xslow gate to be executed, there is no need for the class to be `XSlowGate`, as along as the gate name is `xslow`.

About the qasm3 exporter, the solution of a dummy definition to make the exporter happy can be problematic, because the definition is used in transpilation. For example this code runs, where I'd want it to fail (it fails if we omit the line that sets a definition):
```python
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit, transpile
from qiskit_ibm_runtime import QiskitRuntimeService
from qiskit_ibm_runtime.circuit.library import XSlowGate


backend = QiskitRuntimeService().backend("ibm_boston")

xslow = XSlowGate()
xslow.definition = QuantumCircuit(1)

qc = QuantumCircuit(1, 1)
qc.append(xslow, [0])
qc.measure(0, 0)

transpile(qc, basis_gates=["cz", "id", "rz", "sx", "x"])
```

I checked a bit the options of registering a gate to qasm3, and it doesn't look promising. We can instruct our users to set the `basis_gates` argument of `dump` and `dumps`, but we seek for a solution that will not require anything from the users. We can monkey-patch `dumps`, but it will be ugly.

@jakelishman Can you please try to propose something? TL;DR it appears that `definition` has two different usages: one for the transpiler and another one for the qasm3 exporter. We want the definition to be `None` for the transpiler to work properly, but then it makes the qasm3 exporter fail.

> We can instruct our users to set the `basis_gates` argument of [`qasm3`'s] `dump` and `dumps`

This is the correct solution.  `xslow` is not a gate in OQ3, so Qiskit can't decide to export a symbol with no definition without user input.  The override for that is `basis_gates`, which means "treat this symbol as externally defined".  Note also that Qiskit (and any other general-purpose OQ3 parser) will refuse to load an OQ3 file like this because it's invalid without a definition - you have to be using a special parser that knows to expect `xslow` as defined elsewhere.

Other gates, like `x`, typically work because they're in the default `stdgates.inc` include file, and Qiskit emits an include statement for that by default.

> QPY doesn't preserve the `XSlowGate` subclass.

This is the defined behaviour of QPY.  We explicitly _don't_ allow the QPY file itself to specify classes/constructors for objects that are not owned by Qiskit SDK itself, for security reasons.

Are you encountering any issues because the subclass is not retained?  In general, it should be sufficient to examine the gate name.  If you are, we can potentially discuss feature additions.
